prose.def: Swept away or carried off by a river or flood.

prose.def: An interrogative word asking what sort, kind, or quality something is.

prose.def: An indefinite time-word meaning "at some time," used either of the past ("formerly," "once") or, after a negative or question, "ever."
prose.article: ποτέ is a small, unstressed particle that points vaguely at a moment in time rather than naming one — "at some time," "once," "formerly." Most of its measured renderings cluster around describing what people or things used to be ("were," "once were," "formerly"), and after a negative or in a question it shifts to mean "ever." Because it leans on surrounding words, it often disappears into the English phrasing entirely — 7 of its 29 Byzantine occurrences carry no separate English word. The papyri show the same flavor: P Fay 110 calls a man "the former president" (τόν ποτε ἡγούμενον).
prose.caution: Its meaning depends heavily on context, so the many overlapping renderings ("were," "once," "formerly") reflect translation choices rather than sharply distinct senses.

prose.def: A thing done or being dealt with — a deed, action, matter, affair, or legal case.

prose.def: A word marking that one event happened earlier than another — "before" something else occurred.

prose.def: A preposition (with the genitive) meaning before — earlier in time, or positioned in front of someone or something in space.

prose.def: To get something ready ahead of time; to arrange or complete a preparation in advance.
prose.article: This verb combines "before" (πρό) with "to make ready" (καταρτίζω), so it means to prepare or arrange something beforehand. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 9:5, where Paul sends people ahead to get the promised collection ready in advance. The lexicons agree on "make ready beforehand," though notice the Majority Standard Bible renders the surrounding phrase with "gift" — that reflects the object being prepared rather than the verb's own meaning of advance preparation.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range rests on a single passage.

prose.def: To be set out or placed in front of someone, whether a goal, an offer, or something already present.
prose.article: πρόκειμαι is built from πρό ("before") and κεῖμαι ("to lie"), so it literally means "to lie before" — something laid out in plain view, whether a hope, a race, a joy, or an offering. In the New Testament's 5 occurrences it covers both a thing set before someone (Hebrews 6:18; 12:1-2) and what a person already has on hand (2 Corinthians 8:12). The everyday Koine papyri use the participle constantly to mean "aforesaid" or "the above-mentioned," as in a contract to purchase "the office of prophet in the aforesaid temple" — a practical legal sense.
prose.caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences spread across 3 senses, the evidence base is thin for any single nuance.

prose.def: To announce or proclaim something in advance, like a herald giving public notice before an event.
prose.article: This verb combines "before" (πρό) with "to herald" (κηρύσσω), so it means to proclaim something ahead of time. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 13:24, where John the Baptist proclaimed Jesus' coming in advance. The everyday papyri are especially telling here: the word shows up in business and legal contexts meaning to issue a public notice or advertise — for example, one document instructs someone to "issue a public notice and advertize."
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range cannot be measured from usage alone.

prose.def: Forward movement or advancement, especially growth toward a goal—whether personal progress or the way events move things ahead.
prose.article: προκοπή means progress or advancement, an image originally drawn from moving forward on a journey. In the New Testament it appears just 3 times, rendered as "progress" twice (Philippians 1:25; 1 Timothy 4:15) and as "circumstances" once (Philippians 1:12), where the sense is that events have moved things forward. Interestingly, the word is absent from classical Greek and was a technical term in Stoic philosophy for progress toward wisdom; Moulton-Milligan also shows its everyday use in a papyrus letter wishing someone "greater advancement."
prose.caution: With only 3 occurrences and a thin record (the Atticists even condemned the word), this entry rests on limited evidence.

prose.def: To advance or make progress—growing in amount, maturing over time, or moving steadily toward a goal.
prose.article: At its root προκόπτω pictures cutting a way forward, like a pioneer clearing brush, but in later Koine it became wholly intransitive—simply meaning to advance or make progress. It stretches across different kinds of progress: a person maturing (Luke 2:52 "grew in favor"), or time moving along (Romans 13:12 "the night is nearly over"). Everyday papyri show the same flavor: one ii/A.D. soldier writes home that he hopes "to be quickly promoted, if the gods will," while another letter wishes a friend health and continued advancement.
prose.caution: With only 6 occurrences—4 of them dissolved into surrounding phrasing—the measured English range rests on a thin sample.

prose.def: Making a judgment about someone before knowing the facts; deciding for or against a person out of partiality.
prose.article: πρόκριμα means prejudging someone, deciding in their favor or against them before the facts are clear. It appears only once in the Greek Bible, in 1 Timothy 5:21, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "bias" (100% of occurrences), and the BSB agrees. The same phrase used there, χωρὶς προκρίματος ("without prejudgment"), turns up three times in an everyday legal papyrus from A.D. 172, showing this was ordinary Koine used in disputes to mean acting without bias.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Greek Bible, so its range rests on a single verse plus outside papyri evidence.

prose.def: To formally confirm or ratify something in advance, settling it beforehand as a binding agreement.
prose.article: This compound joins "before" (πρό) with "to ratify" (κυρόω), so it means to validate or settle an agreement in advance. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 3:17, where Paul speaks of a covenant established beforehand. Notably, while the lexicons (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) and Strong's all define it as "establish or ratify before," the Majority Standard Bible renders the single occurrence as "revoke" — likely shaped by the surrounding context of a law that cannot annul the prior covenant.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the lexicons ("ratify beforehand") sit oddly against the MSB rendering "revoke," so its precise force rests on very thin evidence.
